Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, use the point mass on the empty-product singleton; if $n=1$, use $K_0(s)$. For $n\ge2$, fix $s\in S$ and build the product recursively: start with $K_0(s)$, and at stage $j+1$ apply [F1] to the probability measure already constructed on the first $j$ factors and the probability measure $K_j(s)$. This constructs a probability measure on the recursively defined first $j+1$ factors, with the product rectangle formula. Finite induction gives $K(s,\cdot)=\bigotimes_{i<n}K_i(s,\cdot)$ and its formula for every $s$.

For a rectangle $R=\prod_{i<n}B_i$, step 1.1 gives $s\mapsto K(s,R)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i)$, a finite product of measurable real functions, hence measurable. Let $\mathcal D$ be the product-measurable sets $E$ for which $s\mapsto K(s,E)$ is measurable. The class contains the whole space and all rectangles. If $E\in\mathcal D$, then $K(s,E^c)=1-K(s,E)$ is measurable. For pairwise disjoint $E_j\in\mathcal D$, countable additivity gives $K(s,\bigcup_jE_j)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j\le N}K(s,E_j)$, a pointwise limit of measurable functions. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system. Rectangles form a pi-system and generate the product sigma-algebra by [F2], so [F4] gives $\mathcal D=\bigotimes_{i<n}\Tau_i$. Hence $K$ is a probability kernel.

Any other probability kernel with the rectangle formula agrees with $K(s,\cdot)$ on the generating rectangle pi-system for each fixed $s$. The measures are finite, so uniqueness [F3] gives equality on the full product sigma-algebra at every $s$. This proves uniqueness, including the empty product case.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

For probability kernels $K:(S,\Sigma)\to(T,\Tau)$ and $L:(T,\Tau)\to(U,\Upsilon)$, their **composition**, in the order K then L, is
$$(KL)(s,A)=\int_T L(t,A)\,K(s,dt),\qquad s\in S,\quad A\in\Upsilon.$$

The kernel convention is [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The integrand is measurable in t and lies in $[0,1]$, so the displayed number exists in $[0,1]$. As a function of s it is measurable by [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]], applied to the product-measurable function $(s,t)\mapsto L(t,A)$: its threshold preimages are rectangles $S\times\{t:L(t,A)>a\}$. The probability-kernel assertion and associativity are justified by [[lem-kernel-composition-is-well-defined-and-associative]].

Composition refers to specified pointwise kernels. Almost-everywhere classes alone do not define this formula until representatives and the relevant measures are specified. For an empty source the candidate is the empty map. No choice of versions or assumption of AC enters this definition.

The composition KL of probability kernels $K:S\to T$ and $L:T\to U$ is a probability kernel $S\to U$. If $M:U\to V$ is another probability kernel, then $(KL)M=K(LM)$ at every source point and every measurable subset of V. Equality concerns the specified kernels, not unspecified almost-everywhere classes.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For fixed parent values $x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}$, the map $u\mapsto f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},u)$ is measurable, so its pushforward of $\nu_v$ is a probability measure. For each measurable $B\subseteq S_v$, $K_v(x,B)$ is the integral of the jointly measurable indicator $1_B(f_v(x,u))$ against the constant probability kernel $x\mapsto\nu_v$; [F2] makes this evaluation measurable in $x$. Hence $K_v$ is a probability kernel, including when the parent set is empty.

By [F1], the joint law of the finite exogenous vector is $\bigotimes_{r=1}^n\nu_{v_r}$. Fix a bounded measurable function $g$ of $X_{v_1},\ldots,X_{v_{r-1}}$ and a measurable set $B\subseteq S_{v_r}$. The recursive construction makes the earlier coordinates functions only of $U_{v_1},\ldots,U_{v_{r-1}}$. Applying Fubini to the bounded indicator integrand and integrating first in $u_{v_r}$ gives $E[g\,1_{\{X_{v_r}\in B\}}] =E[g\,K_{v_r}(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},B)].$ Thus the conditional law of $X_{v_r}$ given the preceding endogenous vector is the stated kernel; its parent coordinates are among that vector by the topological order.

Starting with $v_1$, whose parent set is empty, apply step 1.2 successively for $r=2,\ldots,n$. At each stage the joint law of the first $r$ endogenous coordinates is the composition of the previous joint law with $K_{v_r}$. Associativity and normalization in [F3] make this a probability kernel at each finite stage. Induction therefore gives exactly the displayed topological product for the full vector.

Under $do(X_I=a)$, the coordinates in $I$ are constants and their conditional kernels are $\delta_{a_v}$; every other equation still uses the same independent exogenous coordinate and the same parent values, with an intervened parent replaced by its fixed constant. Repeating step 1.2 with these kernels proves the interventional product. The observed law is the pushforward under coordinate projection; integrating out the latent coordinates is marginalization and creates no asserted observed-only DAG factorization.

A **finite directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a finite vertex set $V$ with an
arrow set $E\subseteq V\times V$ and no directed cycle. A **path** from $u$ to
$v$ is a finite sequence of distinct vertices beginning at $u$ and ending at
$v$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction;
the arrows are not required to point along the sequence. An internal vertex of
a path is a **collider on that path** when the two arrows on the path both point
into it, and is a **noncollider** otherwise. A vertex $w$ is a **descendant** of
$v$ if there is a directed path from $v$ to $w$; for this definition
$\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ includes $v$ itself as well as its descendants.

For pairwise disjoint vertex sets $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, a path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is **active given $C$** when every internal noncollider is outside $C$ and
every internal collider has at least one member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in
$C$. The set $C$ **d-separates** $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ when no path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is active given $C$; write $X\perp_d Y\mid C$ in $G$. The empty set of
vertices is allowed for any of $X,Y,C$; in particular d-separation is vacuous
if either endpoint set is empty.

For $T\subseteq V$, $G_{\underline T}$ is obtained by deleting every arrow
whose tail lies in $T$, and $G_{\overline T}$ by deleting every arrow whose
head lies in $T$. These are graph operations only; they do not by themselves
specify a probability law under intervention.

For $S\subseteq V$, its **ancestral set** is
$$\operatorname{An}_G(S):=\{v\in V:\text{there is a directed path from }v\text{ to some }s\in S\},$$
where paths of length zero are allowed, so $S\subseteq\operatorname{An}_G(S)$.
The induced directed subgraph on this set keeps exactly the arrows of $G$
whose two endpoints lie in $\operatorname{An}_G(S)$. Its **moral graph** is
the undirected simple graph obtained by replacing every arrow by an
undirected edge and joining every distinct pair of parents of a common child
by an undirected edge; loops and duplicate edges are discarded. This
undirected graph is the **ancestral moral graph** on $S$ and is denoted
$\operatorname{mor}_G(S)$.

derivations.claim: Suppose an active path joins $X$ to $Y$. Every internal noncollider on the path has at least one adjacent path-arrow pointing away from it. Follow that arrow along the path; either the directed segment reaches an endpoint or first reaches a collider. In the latter case that collider has a directed descendant in $C$ by [F1]. An internal collider already lies in $\operatorname{An}_G(C)$ by activity, and the path endpoints lie in $X\cup Y$. Hence every vertex on the path lies in $\operatorname{An}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$. Whenever the path enters and leaves a collider $w$ as $u\to w\leftarrow v$, replace the two edges by the moral edge $u-v$. Every noncollider on the resulting walk lies outside $C$ by [F1], and each collider itself has been removed. The walk therefore gives an undirected connection from $X$ to $Y$ in the ancestral moral graph with $C$ deleted.

Conversely, take a shortest undirected path from $X$ to $Y$ in the ancestral moral graph with $C$ deleted. Replace each edge that joins two parents of a common child $w$ and is not a skeleton edge by the two-edge route $u\to w\leftarrow v$. The resulting finite route in $G$ has all noncolliders outside $C$ because the original path avoids $C$; every collider introduced by a replacement is an ancestor of $X\cup Y\cup C$ by [F2]. Colliders that are ancestors of $C$ are active. If an introduced collider $w$ is not an ancestor of $C$, then it is an ancestor of $X$ or $Y$. Follow a directed path from $w$ to that endpoint and splice it into the route, replacing the segment on that endpoint's side of $w$. The new segment has only noncolliders, none in $C$ (otherwise $w$ would be an ancestor of $C$), and makes $w$ a noncollider. Delete any closed subroute at its first repeated vertex; this retains the endpoints and removes, but does not create, a collider on the directed replacement segment. Choosing a route with the fewest nonactivated collider occurrences, and then the fewest edges, shows that the splicing process terminates with an active path. More explicitly, the splice deletes the portion from the selected endpoint to $w$ and replaces it by a directed chain from $w$ to a vertex of $X$ or $Y$, traversed in reverse. The retained incidence at $w$ has one arrow entering and one leaving, so $w$ is no longer a collider. Every interior vertex of the replacement chain is a noncollider and is outside $C$. If the chain meets the retained route, erase the closed segment between its first repeated vertex; the directed segment contributes no collider, and the retained incidences are those of the route at that vertex. Thus the complexity pair (number of nonactivated colliders, then length) strictly decreases. It terminates with an active route; removing any remaining repeated-vertex loop by the same first-repeat argument gives an active path. Hence an undirected connection implies an active path.

The two implications show that an active path exists exactly when the ancestral moral graph with $C$ removed connects $X$ to $Y$. Negating both sides gives the claimed equivalence. If $X$ or $Y$ is empty both path conditions are false, so the equivalence still holds.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable

$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$

representatives.

$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that

the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

derivations.claim: Put $S=A\cup B\cup C$ and $W=\operatorname{An}_G(S)$. Integrate vertices outside $W$ out of the topological product in reverse topological order. Each such vertex has no descendant in $S$ and its own conditional kernel integrates to one, so the marginal law on $W$ retains the product of the kernels indexed by $W$. This uses normalization and finite iterated kernel composition from [F4]; no observed-only or latent-marginal factorization is inferred.

Delete $C$ from the moral graph on $W$ and partition the remaining vertices into connected components. By [F1], no component contains both a vertex of $A$ and a vertex of $B$. For any vertex $v$ in one component, every parent of $v$ is either in that same component or in $C$: a parent is joined to $v$ by a skeleton edge, and two parents of $v$ are joined by [F2]. Thus each component's local factors depend only on its own coordinates and the fixed separator coordinates $x_C$.

For each component $D$, compose its local kernels in the inherited topological order, treating $x_C$ as fixed inputs. By [F4] this defines a probability kernel $Q_D(x_C,dx_D)$. By [F3], the finitely many component kernels have a product kernel $Q(x_C,d(x_D)_D)$. Finite Fubini [F6] reorders the component integrations. On measurable rectangles, the conditional joint law of all coordinates in $W\setminus C$ given $X_C=x_C$ therefore equals $Q(x_C,\cdot)$; uniqueness on the generating rectangle pi-system in [F6] extends this identity to the product sigma-algebra.

Group the components meeting $A$ into $D_A$, those meeting $B$ into $D_B$, and all other components into $D_0$. The groups $D_A$ and $D_B$ are disjoint by step 2.1. These are versions because testing either one against every event in $\sigma(X_C)$ recovers the corresponding marginal integral by step 3.1. This is exactly conditional independence by [F5]. If $A$ or $B$ is empty, its function is constant and the same identity holds.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $Y^a$ and $A$ are conditionally independent given $L$. By [F2] take regular conditional laws of $Y^a$ given $L$ and given $(A,L)$. Since $a$ is an atom with $e_a(l)>0$ for $P_L$-almost every $l$, the measure $P_{L\mid A=a}$ is equivalent to $P_L$: its density with respect to $P_L$ is $e_a(l)/P(A=a)$, which is positive and integrates to one. Hence the conditional-law equality at $A=a$ holds for $P_L$-almost every $l$.

On the event $A=a$, the factual structural recursion and the recursion with the $A$ equation replaced by $a$ agree at $A$. Induction down the fixed topological order shows that they agree at every descendant, in particular $Y=Y^a$. Therefore the conditional law of $Y^a$ given $A=a,L=l$ equals that of $Y$ given $A=a,L=l$ for $P_L$-almost every $l$. Combining with step 1.1 identifies the conditional law of $Y^a$ given $L=l$ with the observed conditional law in the formula.

Disintegrating the joint law of $(Y^a,L)$ by [F2] gives $P(Y^a\in B)=\int P(Y^a\in B\mid L=l)P_L(dl)$. Substitute the equality from step 2.1 to obtain the displayed formula. If two SCM parameter values induce the same observed law, the integrand kernel and $P_L$ agree outside their common null sets; positivity makes those sets null for the target integral. Hence the right side, and so the estimand, is constant on each observational-equivalence class by [F4]. The real-valued expectation formula follows by applying the distribution identity to bounded truncations of $Y$ and using integrability to pass to the limit.

It is retained in $G_{\underline A}$, because the path uses no arrow out of its endpoint $A$, and is active given the empty set. This contradicts (ii), so $I_M\cap I_A=\varnothing$.

It lies in $G_{\underline M}$ and is active given $\{A\}$, contradicting (iii). Thus $I_M\cap I_Y=\varnothing$.

It avoids $M$ by definition and avoids $A$, because an occurrence of $A$ would leave a directed $A$-to-$Y$ suffix avoiding $M$, contrary to (i). Thus $q$ is retained in $G_{\underline M}$. If an active path $p$ from $M$ to $v$ given $\{A\}$ existed there, choose the last vertex $w$ of $p$ that also lies on $q$ when $q$ is traversed from $v$ to $Y$. Keep the prefix of $p$ from $M$ to $w$ and append the directed suffix of $q$ from $w$ to $Y$. The suffix after $w$ is disjoint from the prefix by the choice of $w$, so this is a path. Its old internal vertices remain active; $w\notin A$ and the outgoing directed edge makes it a noncollider; all new internal vertices are noncolliders outside $A$. This would be an active path from $M$ to $Y$ given $A$, contradicting (iii). Hence $A$ d-separates $M$ and $v$ in $G_{\underline M}$. Since the added exogenous root $U_v$ has only the child edge $U_v\to v$, $A$ also d-separates $M$ and the whole root set $U_{I_Y}$ in the expanded graph with arrows out of $M$ deleted.
By [F3], the disjoint exogenous vectors $U_{I_M}$ and $U_{I_A}$ are independent. Step 1.1 makes $M^a$ and factual $A$ measurable functions of these respective vectors, so $M^a\perp A$.

The finite vectors $U_{I_M}$ and $U_{I_Y}$ are independent by [F3]. By step 1.1, $M^a$ and the response family $(Y^m)_{m\in S_M}$ are measurable functions of these disjoint vectors; in particular $M^a\perp U_{I_Y}$.

Adjoin all exogenous coordinates as independent root vertices. In the factual law, no strict descendant of $M$ is an ancestor of $(M,A,U_{I_Y})$: it cannot be an ancestor of an exogenous root, and if it were an ancestor of $A$, the directed path from $M$ to $A$ would remain in $G_{\underline A}$ and contradict (ii). Reverse-topological integration therefore marginalizes all other vertices and leaves the joint law of $(M,A,U_{I_Y})$ factored on its ancestral subgraph, which has no outgoing edge from $M$. This is a subgraph of the expanded mutilated graph in step 1.4, so the separation there still holds. The global Markov implication [F2], interpreted by the conditional-independence definition [F4], gives $M\perp U_{I_Y}\mid A$.

In $G_{\overline M}$ there is no directed path from $A$ to $Y$, since every directed $A$-to-$Y$ path in $G$ contains $M$ and arrows into $M$ were deleted. With $M$ fixed, changing the equation at $A$ therefore cannot change $Y$ by recursive substitution: any directed route by which $A$ could affect $Y$ would have to reach the fixed node $M$. Under $do(A=a)$, the mediator equals $M^a$. Replacing the mediator equation by that same realized value leaves every other equation unchanged; the no-directed-path argument shows that leaving $A$ factual has no further effect on $Y$. Thus $Y^a=Y^{M^a}$.

Assume AC and a finite Markovian recursive SCM on a full DAG with observed
vertices $A,M,Y$ and any number of latent vertices. Suppose: (i) every
directed path from $A$ to $Y$ contains $M$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are
d-separated by the empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$
d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in $G_{\underline M}$. For each supplied value
$a\in S_A$, let $M^a$ be the response under $do(A=a)$. Define
$$I_M=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline A}}(M)\setminus\{A\},\qquad I_Y=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline M}}(Y)\setminus\{M\},$$
where ancestry includes the vertex itself and $U_I$ is the finite vector of
exogenous coordinates $(U_v)_{v\in I}$. Then $M^a$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_M})$, each response $Y^m$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_Y})$, and
$$M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp A,\qquad I_M\cap I_Y=\varnothing,\qquad M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y},\qquad M\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y}\mid A.$$
The recursive responses also satisfy $Y^a=Y^{M^a}$ almost surely. The
conditional independence is for the factual law; it supplies a genuine
conditional product law for the exogenous coordinates used by the outcome
response.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Assume AC. Let X,Y take values in standard-Borel E,T, and let K be a disintegration kernel giving the conditional law of X given Y. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, put $h(y)=\int_E f(x)K(y,dx)$. Then h is measurable and
$$E[f(X)\mid\sigma(Y)]=h(Y)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For measurable real f with $E|f(X)|<\infty$, define $D=\{y:\int|f(x)|K(y,dx)<\infty\}$ and use the signed integral for h on D, zero off D. Then $P_Y(D)=1$, h is real measurable, and the same identity holds.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.

For each supported atom $a'$, let $

The treatment support is countable, so the intersection of these sets is still $\mu_a$-full. The integrability hypothesis and the nonnegative identity in step 1.1 imply $\int\!\int |F(m,u)|\,
u_{a'}(du)\,P_A(da')\,\mu_a(dm)<\infty.$ Since $A$ is countable-valued, the law of $U_{I_Y}$ is the mixture $
u=\int
u_{a'}P_A(da')$. Hence $\int\!\int|F(m,u)|\,
u(du)\,\mu_a(dm)<\infty,$ and the conditional mean kernel has the observed-law representation $\int F(m,u)\,

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

A **finite directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a finite vertex set $V$ with an
arrow set $E\subseteq V\times V$ and no directed cycle. A **path** from $u$ to
$v$ is a finite sequence of distinct vertices beginning at $u$ and ending at
$v$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction;
the arrows are not required to point along the sequence. An internal vertex of
a path is a **collider on that path** when the two arrows on the path both point
into it, and is a **noncollider** otherwise. A vertex $w$ is a **descendant** of
$v$ if there is a directed path from $v$ to $w$; for this definition
$\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ includes $v$ itself as well as its descendants.

For pairwise disjoint vertex sets $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, a path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is **active given $C$** when every internal noncollider is outside $C$ and
every internal collider has at least one member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in
$C$. The set $C$ **d-separates** $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ when no path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is active given $C$; write $X\perp_d Y\mid C$ in $G$. The empty set of
vertices is allowed for any of $X,Y,C$; in particular d-separation is vacuous
if either endpoint set is empty.

For $T\subseteq V$, $G_{\underline T}$ is obtained by deleting every arrow
whose tail lies in $T$, and $G_{\overline T}$ by deleting every arrow whose
head lies in $T$. These are graph operations only; they do not by themselves
specify a probability law under intervention.

Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values
$X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$; the interventional law is their joint law. The
response map $(a,\omega)\mapsto X_w^a(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, by
induction through the finite topological order and joint measurability of each
$f_v$. This permits evaluation at a random treatment value, such as
$X_w^{M^a}$. When $I=\{A\}$, write $X_w^a$ for the response under
$do(A=a)$. If the factual treatment is $A$, then on $\{A=a\}$ recursion
gives $X_w=X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$.

derivations.claim: In the confounding model, $P(A=1)=P(U=0,E=1)+P(U=1,E=0)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac12$. Also $P(U=1,A=1)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac38$ and $P(U=1,A=0)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac18$. Thus $P(Y=1\mid A=1)=3/4$ and $P(Y=1\mid A=0)=1/4$, although under $do(A=a)$ the variable $Y=U$ remains Bernoulli$(1/2)$. The difference between the observational conditionals and the intervention law is caused by the open backdoor path through $U$; conditioning on $U$ blocks that path and the adjusted mean is $\sum_{u\in\{0,1\}}P(Y=1\mid A=a,U=u)P(U=u)=1/2$.

For the collider model, $P(B=1,C=1)=1/4=P(B=1)P(C=1)$ by [F1], so the variables are independent before conditioning. But $D=1$ on exactly the three equiprobable pairs $(1,1),(1,0),(0,1)$. Hence $P(B=1\mid D=1)=P(C=1\mid D=1)=2/3$ while $P(B=1,C=1\mid D=1)=1/3\ne4/9$. Conditioning on the collider $D$ therefore creates dependence, exactly as the active-path rule [F2] predicts.

required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly

$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$

$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.

$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume AC and a finite Markovian SCM with observed countable-valued
treatment $A$, observed standard-Borel mediator $M$, and real outcome $Y$.
Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$. Suppose in the full DAG: (i) $M$ lies on
every directed path from $A$ to $Y$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are d-separated by the
empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$ d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in
$G_{\underline M}$. Write $\mu_a=P(M\in\cdot\mid A=a)$ and, for every
positive-probability treatment atom $a'$, write
$\mu_{a'}=P(M\in\cdot\mid A=a')$. Assume the nested-law support condition
$$\mu_a\ll\mu_{a'}\qquad\text{for every }a'\text{ with }P(A=a')>0,$$
and absolute integrability of the nested conditional means:
$$\int\!\int E(|Y|\mid M=m,A=a')\,P_A(da')\,\mu_a(dm)<\infty.$$
Then
$$E[Y^a]=\int P(dm\mid A=a)\int E(Y\mid M=m,A=a')\,P_A(da').$$
The right side is determined by the observed law, so the interventional mean
is identifiable on any statistical model of SCMs satisfying these
assumptions. For a discrete mediator, the support condition says that every
mediator value having positive probability under $A=a$ also has positive
probability under every positive-probability treatment atom. These are
sufficient conditions only. For non-atomic treatment values, regular
conditional formulas are determined only $P_A$-almost everywhere; this
item makes no pointwise claim at a null treatment value.

derivations.claim: Since $P(A=1)=1/2$, Bayes' rule gives $P(U=1\mid A=1)=3/4$ and $P(U=1\mid A=0)=1/4$. Since $E_M$ is independent of $(U,A)$, $P(M=1\mid A=1)=4/5$ and $P(M=1\mid A=0)=1/5$. Thus for each $a\in\{0,1\}$ both mediator outcomes have positive conditional probability; the nested-law support condition in [F2] holds.

If $M=1$, then $Y=1$. If $M=0$, then $Y=U$, so $E(Y\mid M=0,A=1)=3/4$ and $E(Y\mid M=0,A=0)=1/4$. Averaging over the marginal law of $A$ gives $\int E(Y\mid M=0,A=a')P_A(da')=1/2$, while the same inner average for $M=1$ is $1$. The front-door formula [F2] therefore gives $\tfrac45\cdot1+\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac9{10}.$

Under $do(A=1)$, $M=1$ with probability $4/5$ and $M=0$ with probability $1/5$. The exogenous $U$ remains Bernoulli$(1/2)$ and independent of $E_M$, so $E(Y\mid do(A=1),M=1)=1$ and $E(Y\mid do(A=1),M=0)=1/2$. Hence $E[Y^{1}]=\tfrac45\cdot1+\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac12=9/10$, agreeing with the observed functional.
